title: Landscapes of Unfinished Obligation
summary: Independent atmospheric histories extend burial terraces, cargo disturbance, a contested battlefield, and the submerged stair while preserving finite costs and uncertain testimony.

entries.title: The Terraces of the Second Foot
entries.inspiration: Original burial landscape connecting the fallen shelf empire, competing succession, and visible salt forms to the bodily division of incompatible undertakings.
entries.body:
The burial terraces face east because the old shelf court promised each named grave the first water carried from the morning cistern. This was once a small undertaking: twenty-seven graves, twenty-seven cups, one household assigned to each. The court subsequently added soldiers, servants, and relatives by declaring them members of those households. When its dominion broke apart in 349, three successor offices inherited different lists. They continued pouring water into the same stone mouths.

The terraces did not rise from the ground. Their walls remained where the masons built them. What changed was the descent. A bearer walking down after the morning observance felt a second footfall beside the first, close enough to seem their own and always half a pace late. Some bearers began putting one foot on the step above and the other on the step below, unable to complete either movement. The earliest account describes a woman holding a cup for seven hours while her brother cut its leather sling. Releasing the cup let her sit; returning to the staircase restored the divided act.

The present route uses wooden crossings between levels. Custodians pour each lineage's water on separate mornings, allowing the lower cistern to recover between them. This has reduced the divided movements without establishing which successor office possesses the better claim. Anyone visiting the terraces can see the expense: worn planks, ropes hung to dry, and garden rows shortened because burial water still has to come from somewhere. The poor dead receive no more water by becoming numerous in a court's account.

Lonsha's salt readers have mapped branching deposits around the old stone mouths. Their drawings suggest three different channels feed two of the graves claimed by all three lists. They have requested permission to expose the junction. One office fears damage to the observance; another fears evidence that would weaken its genealogy. The third has offered money for an investigation whose conclusion it would approve in advance. The readers refused that condition.

In 1248, an unclaimed infant's grave remains outside the terraces beneath a repaired pear tree. Its neighbors maintain it without asserting that affection supplies ancestral title. People sometimes call that grave the only free place on the shelf. The phrase is too easy. The tree needs pruning, the marker needs shelter, and someone carries water even there. Yet the care can still be offered for one season and renewed by choice. The terrace bearers stop beside it before entering the old obligations, both feet on the same earth.

entries.title: The Cargo That Arrived as a Forest
entries.inspiration: Original maritime horror drawn from spice-source concealment and political praise, connected to the distinction between soil possession and channel obligations.
entries.body:
The cargo arrived as bundled bark, wrapped in coarse cloth and loaded beneath sacks of millet. It never became a living forest. The familiar name comes from the warehouse keepers' account: while the bark remained inside, footsteps sounded among trunks, ropes rasped against unseen branches, and a person searching for the far wall sometimes returned with scratches no surviving beam could explain. The warehouse measured seventeen ordinary paces across. None of the scratches contained a thorn.

The bark had been stripped at a landing whose sellers insisted upon naming the growing households in every subsequent sale. A Talassari intermediary erased those names to protect the source from competitors. He retained their witnessed promise to supply the next harvest while representing the cargo as his own unrestricted possession. The expedition's water jar, used to authenticate delivery, traveled with the bundles. Whether that combination caused the disturbance remains disputed; inspection established it before anybody proposed an explanation.

Opening the doors and removing six bundles quieted one corner. Burning a bundle brought ordinary smoke and worsened the voices heard near the floor. The keepers then separated the cargo into dry sheds and sent the jar back with an account of its custody. They paid for three named witnesses to travel from the producers' landing. During the resulting inventory, the sounds dwindled until only one faint rope scrape remained beside a repaired drain. The drain lost water for the rest of the season. The missing volume could be measured. A punishment could not.

Grosen painted the governor standing before an open warehouse, with invented healthy trees behind him. The picture implied that the visiting ruler had made abundance safe through courage. It omitted the keepers' soaked bedding, the failed burn, and the suppliers who returned to correct the account. Orven's lament was commissioned for the same welcome feast. He sang without moving, naming the distance a household must travel to recover a word erased by someone richer. Several patrons left before the final verse.

In 1248 the warehouse contains net floats and spare planking. Boat crews knock on its threshold before entering, a habit with no verified supernatural effect. The old cloth wraps survive in the cargo readers' room, each attached to a plain statement of where it was used. Traders still sell extravagant accounts of a bark forest hidden beyond the sea. Pilots prefer the recorded route, whose hazards include bad weather and unpaid suppliers. The surviving scrape is heard chiefly after heavy rain. A mason believes a loose fitting explains it; the keeper leaves both accounts open and repairs the drain.

entries.title: The Plateau of Open Mouths
entries.inspiration: Original aftermath linking an ambiguously decisive coalition battle with an oracle, air inquiry, and material care for travelers.
entries.body:
The mouths are neither human remains nor statues. They are low clay vents set above old underground storage pits on the plateau. During the coalition battle of 472, cooks used the pits to keep grain cool and wounded people sheltered from sun. Later victory accounts describe them as the places where fallen ancestors swallowed an invading king's breath. The cooks' surviving tallies record beans, smoke, and inadequate bedding. They also record a sound that nobody present could place: one long exhalation from a pit already emptied.

After the armies departed, the local shrine claimed the sound as an oracle's confirmation that the coalition had saved the basin. Families whose dead came from different sides were offered commemorative places only if they accepted that wording. Several declined. They built low stone shelters around the pits where their relatives had actually been tended, marking names without endorsing a shared explanation for the battle. Some shelters remain; others supplied stone for the winter hospice when its first roof failed.

Travelers still encounter the exhalation at particular vents. It extinguishes a small flame held close to the opening and leaves frost on a wet cord even during warm weather. Removing the cord ends that visible effect. Air keepers have compared empty pits, shaded pits, and pits with different amounts of moisture. The accounts support a local disturbance, not a voice that can pronounce upon the legitimacy of every ruler passing through. No traveler has reliably extracted a word from it. Several profitable guides have claimed otherwise.

The most serious cost is exhaustion. A person sleeping beside an active vent can wake unable to complete an ordinary breath without turning toward the opening. Hospice workers move sufferers to the sheltered western path and take turns keeping them awake until the habit loosens. Recovery can take days. Nobody requires a confession from the afflicted. The plateau's reminders are dangerous regardless of whether a visitor's ancestors fought there, and efforts to treat ancestry as a medical explanation have delayed useful care.

In 1248 pilgrims tie strips of plain cloth to three poles above the old supply camp. Each strip represents a journey completed home, rather than an enemy defeated. Shrine officials tolerate the practice because travelers buy meals nearby, though they dislike its refusal to produce a victorious lineage. On quiet evenings, the poles knock against one another while the vents below remain still. When an exhalation does come, the cloth does not move. The hospice door opens, a lantern is shaded, and somebody carries blankets uphill.

entries.title: The Stair Built for a Drowned Court
entries.inspiration: Original submerged architecture combining successor claims, bounded human exploration, salt observation, and evidence of successive use.
entries.body:
Liwen saw only six steps. Those who publish pictures of a complete drowned palace have invented the remainder. The visible stair descends from a platform beneath the deep cistern, turns behind a square support, and continues beyond the range of light brought under his inverted bell. Its upper tread bears a groove made by something repeatedly dragged across it. The groove does not establish a throne, a coffin, or a particular ruler's passage.

Small pale fish rested above the lower tread during his first inspection. When the rope crew lifted the bell, they followed its shadow and dispersed at the cistern's shallower wall. This ordinary behavior appears in the crew's account beside an extraordinary observation: Liwen's lamp reflection descended one more step after he had stopped moving. He turned the lamp away and the reflection vanished. Neither he nor the surface watchers saw a person beneath him. A subsequent trial with an empty lamp cage produced nothing comparable.

The harbor successor court seized upon the stair as the entrance to its lost ancestral seat. Its oldest shore recitation mentions a square support and six obligations, a resemblance interesting enough to investigate and insufficient to establish title. Salt readers have found deposits at the recovered edge unlike those on the present cistern roof. The difference could indicate an older water regime or stone reused from another place. The Painted Quarter's layered foundations have already shown how persuasive an apparent age can become when later builders carry old material into a new arrangement.

A third inspection was proposed in 1230 and canceled after the rope passed through a cracked guide ring. The apprentice responsible for checking the ring received public blame. The crew ledger showed that a patron had declined its replacement because the ceremonial bell already exceeded the budget. Recording that refusal has done more to preserve later divers than any invocation of the supposed court below. The broken ring hangs in the preparation shelter, wrapped so its edge cannot cut a visitor.

In 1248 the upper stair remains submerged. Custodians permit diagrams of the inspected portion and mark the rest with open space. Their restraint has become unfashionable: collectors prefer a complete palace, and some interpreters sell an account of six drowned rulers who await the right descendant. Liwen has not endorsed it. He describes the cold, the limited air, the fish, the moving reflection, and the moment he asked to be raised. The ruin's unresolved extent is enough to trouble sleep. Nobody needs to furnish it with a finished dynasty.
